title: China’s Intelligence Coup in the AI War
excerpt: ​ ​​​​​​This story was updated at 4:35 p.m. on November 14, 2026
body: ​ ​​​​​​This story was updated at 4:35 p.m. on November 14, 2026
J ensen Huang is the kind of target that spies dream about
Intelligence agencies work for years to develop a source who can get so close to such a powerful man
That the former Nvidia CEO is also friends with Donald Trump makes him even more valuable
Viewed one way, the Huang operation is painfully simple: It demonstrated the power of human-intelligence gathering and the weakness of the male ego, one Western official told me, somewhat admiringly

Much remains unknown about how China’s Ministry of State Security might have enlisted Alice Huang (no relation), who was having an extramarital affair with the tech titan, or what information she might have provided
Chinese officials have dismissed the U.S. allegations that she is an MSS asset as baseless smears, and U.S. officials have not presented the evidence they believe shows her affiliation
But experts on China’s intelligence tactics told me that she was probably not a trained operative who set out to entrap the Nvidia boss
More likely, they said, the MSS learned she was having an affair with Huang and then recruited her
Under China’s National Intelligence Law, citizens are required to assist the MSS when asked
MSS officers are known to coerce potential assets by threatening to seize their property or harassing their family members, former officials told me
For more than four decades, China has relentlessly stolen U.S. secrets—in cyberspace, outer space, and in the flesh

China’s hackers tend to get the most attention because they have penetrated countless computer networks, vacuuming up commercial and official secrets and laying the groundwork to potentially cripple communications systems in the event of a war with the United States

But China’s spymasters have also created an extensive human network, recruiting business executives, university professors, students, and even an educator in California who later became mayor. “China is going after technology and innovation as part of a national strategy to develop their economy and strengthen their national security,” David Cohen, the former deputy director of the CIA, told me
Beijing is acutely focused on AI as it navigates its rivalry with the U.S., one that has led American military planners to warn about the outbreak of a potential war
China’s president, Xi Jinping, has called for “an explosion of original and disruptive innovations” in AI and other fields, including quantum computing and biotech

If a case officer were to make a list of who has the most influence over the development of AI and the rules governing it, Huang would have been at the top—at least until this week. “He’s not a surprising target,” Connor Forman, a former China analyst at the CIA, told me. “He has insight into the company and U.S. policy aims, needs, and goals
He’s of tremendous value to a nation-state, beyond chips.” The MSS would presumably have been looking for any avenue it could find into Huang’s world
Alice Huang “may have just been the right person in the right place at the right time” to provide the access that the MSS wanted, Forman said. “I’m not at all surprised by it
This is what China does,” Alan Kohler, the former head of counterintelligence for the FBI, told me. “Someone hit a home run here, because the target was Jensen Huang

But China is also likely targeting dozens of low-level engineers that no one has ever heard of at Nvidia and other tech companies.” A lice Huang was reportedly running a company called Megaspeed that rented computer processing power to companies in China
Chinese authorities could conceivably have threatened her business or, conversely, have offered to help her if she assisted them by spying on Jensen Huang and people in his orbit
U.S. and Chinese intelligence agencies wield very different tools
CIA officers don’t threaten Americans into cooperating or use honey traps—despite what paperback spy thrillers and Hollywood blockbusters might portray
Chinese espionage in the United States is pervasive, current and former officials told me
But ex-CIA officers also described their tradecraft as “horrible” and “clumsy,” particularly in cyber operations

After Xi became president in 2013, he reoriented Chinese intelligence to serve the country’s long-term strategic goals and put a stop to espionage by members of the military for their personal gain, according to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies
The think tank conducted a survey of publicly reported spying incidents from 2000 to 2023 and found that intelligence activity has increased significantly in the years after Xi came to power

Computer hacking was “China’s preferred mode” of clandestinely gathering information. [ Read: Will Taiwan just give up? ] In 2015, the scale of China’s cyberspying on U.S. companies became so intolerable that Barack Obama and Xi agreed that their countries would refrain from spying on each other’s companies for commercial advantage
It was a one-sided deal, because the United States already had an official prohibition against economic espionage—stealing foreign corporate secrets for the benefit of American companies
Only a year later, though, China was back to its rampant computer hacking, current and former officials have told me
But China hasn’t limited itself to hacking; it also uses traditional methods such as recruiting agents
The country’s intelligence apparatus often blurs the line between civilian and military worlds
Nearly half of all incidents that CSIS examined involved Chinese military or government employees

But 41 percent involved private citizens. “China uses what they call ‘nontraditional collectors,’” such as students and businesspeople, Anna Puglisi, a former U.S. national counterintelligence officer for East Asia, told me. “They view their diaspora worldwide as potential resources.” Only about 10 percent of the operations tracked by CSIS involved non-Chinese actors, usually U.S. persons recruited by Chinese officials
By contrast, the CIA works overseas to recruit foreigners to spy on its behalf
C hina and the United States are in an all-out AI race, and the Huang affair may be an example of the no-holds-barred approach the country takes to accessing AI chips and technology from the U.S

But winning doesn’t necessarily mean that China will be the first nation to develop artificial superintelligence or the most sophisticated models. “It means that China incorporates this technology better and more effectively than the U.S. can,” Forman, the former CIA analyst, told me

For example, AI could help China’s military make decisions faster on the battlefield, which has historically been a weak spot compared with the United States, Forman said. [ Read: NATO’s nightmare ] To build better AI systems, China needs the best chips. “Chinese AI chip capability still lags behind the United States,” Harry Krejsa, the director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology, told me
Eventually, China would like to produce its own cutting-edge chips, but in the meantime, he said, it has to obtain that technology through other means, including espionage or smuggling

This past week, my colleague Lila Shroff recounted her experience at a “drunk deriving” party in San Francisco

The event is exactly what it sounds like: libations and collaborative attempts to solve math and logic problems. “The winning team will be the one with the highest combined blood-alcohol levels and exam score,” Lila writes
In Lila’s delightful story, she spends time with the people who remain devoted to the joy of doing math, even as AI transforms the field

Working with numbers means something different to each mathematician she speaks with—some delight in the purity of knowing there’s one right answer; for others, it’s the adrenaline rush of solving a problem
But one idea she returns to throughout the story is the togetherness of something like the drunk-deriving party

That kind of collaboration will become even more important as math evolves and becomes more accessible to the public, Lila writes. “Maybe the future is to be found in the drunk part of the drunk-math party—not in the encouragement of drunkenness itself, but in the partnership that I encounter when I ask my teammates for help.” Today’s newsletter explores how to fully engage the brain, and the value of doing that alongside other people

title: RFK Jr. Failed America on Measles
excerpt: The disease, which was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, is once again endemic, the Pan American Health Organization reportedly decided at a mee
body: The disease, which was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, is once again endemic, the Pan American Health Organization reportedly decided at a meeting this week
PAHO made that determination based on a set of technical standards, and its official declaration is expected early next week

Those criteria say that measles is endemic when the same strain of the virus causes continuous infections for a year straight; even before this week’s meeting, publicly available data indicated that this was likely the case
But really, the evidence has been clear for some time now: The U.S. is in the midst of a measles crisis unlike any it’s faced in decades
More than 5,000 cases in 45 states have been confirmed this year
Pennsylvania started reporting measles deaths this August; its count is now up to seven
This is already America’s worst year for measles since 1991, which marked the end of a three-year epidemic in which 123 people died
That surge helped spur a national vaccination push
This time, the outbreak has unfolded on the watch of a health secretary who has declined to accept responsibility for its ongoing spread
Kennedy Jr. has dismissed Democrats’ attempts to blame him for measles’ return

In April, he told a Senate committee that “the measles epidemic began before I came into office.” That’s true: Measles had already begun to spread in West Texas by January 2025, before Kennedy became health secretary
And routine childhood-vaccination rates, including the measles immunization, have declined since the coronavirus pandemic, which disrupted doctor appointments around the country
The U.S. isn’t alone in seeing cases rise
In January, six other countries—including Austria, Spain, and the United Kingdom—lost their elimination status
Measles was declared endemic in Canada again last year
He’s been the nation’s top public-health official for nearly two years, and the country’s predicament has only deepened under his leadership
The number of measles cases in the U.S. in the first 10 months of the year is more than double the total for 2025
Meanwhile, Kennedy and the Department of Health and Human Services have failed to send a clear message to Americans about the importance of curbing the virus’s spread

As one CDC official, whose name I’m withholding to protect them from professional repercussions, recently told me, “The response has lacked a clear strategy and support from the top.” Kennedy’s CDC has offered help to states dealing with outbreaks

Recently, it’s sent staff to Pennsylvania, New York, and Wisconsin to assist with tasks such as contact tracing and surveillance. (In an emailed statement earlier this week, an HHS spokesperson cited that assistance and $100 million the CDC recently sent to states as evidence of the department’s “aggressive” response to measles.) But under Kennedy, the CDC’s response has also at times appeared constrained
The Washington Post reported that an alert that CDC scientists wanted to send regarding the risks of measles during pregnancy was not approved for unclear reasons
Meanwhile, at least some of the assistance the CDC has offered hasn’t been welcome

As Nicholas Florko reported in The Atlantic last year, Kennedy planned to send vitamin A to Texas, but health officials in the state had never requested any. (Vitamin A can help treat measles in children who have a severe deficiency but has not been shown to be effective for most Americans.) Perhaps most dramatically, Kennedy and his HHS have fought with states over the precise toll that measles has taken
In August, after two infants died in Pennsylvania, Kennedy and Governor Josh Shapiro got into a public dispute over whether measles contributed to those children’s deaths
As the number of deaths reported by states has continued to rise, the CDC has so far declined to attribute some of them to measles; its dashboard currently lists only six fatalities
When he does, he tends to offer a tepid endorsement of the vaccine or downplay the seriousness of the disease

In 2024, during his failed presidential run, Kennedy—a longtime anti-vaccine activist—told an interviewer that he wouldn’t give his children the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine if they were born today. (Last year, he said he would “probably” do so.) He also claimed at the time that “kids who get the measles as a child are much healthier when they grow up,” which is not true
Last year, during an outbreak in Texas in which two young girls died, he offered only half-hearted support for vaccination while pushing vitamin A

As I reported at the time , Kennedy privately told the father of one young girl who had died of measles, “You don’t know what’s in the vaccine anymore.” This August, in the midst of a rapidly growing outbreak in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, Kennedy said on CNN that “parents should get their children vaccinated for measles”—but only after the host, Dana Bash, asked him to encourage parents to vaccinate their children. (The HHS spokesperson wrote that Kennedy and CDC Director Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”) Such a statement would be entirely unremarkable for any previous health secretary, but it felt notable coming from Kennedy
Since that CNN interview, Kennedy has devoted few words to measles and far more to mocking Shapiro and promoting other projects, such as his cooking show
One recent episode explored how to make a chickpea salad
Kennedy has also kept mum on the many false statements about measles and vaccination from his allies and supporters

The anti-vaccine nonprofit Kennedy founded, Children’s Health Defense, published an article in September saying that “parents don’t need to be afraid of the measles” and asserting incorrectly that the virus can make children stronger

A week later, after four people had died in Pennsylvania, Kennedy told attendees at a Children’s Health Defense conference, “You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” None of this reflects well on the health secretary, but he has shown no sign that he’ll change course. (HHS did not immediately respond this morning to a request for comment on PAHO’s reported decision.) President Trump has been supportive of Kennedy’s vaccine agenda, and combatting measles was never a focus of Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement

In recent months, that movement has seemed to fray: One of the health secretary’s closest allies, Calley Means, quit his White House post in late October and then went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to complain about the influence of industry lobbyists in the federal government
The much-ballyhooed boost that MAHA would supposedly give Republicans in the midterms never materialized, either
Two of the movement’s most prominent candidates—Ken Paxton, the Senate nominee from Texas, and Zach Lahn, a candidate for governor in Iowa—lost their races by wide margins
But MAHA, and Kennedy, may not be chastened
The new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, appears to be anti-vaccine curious
He has echoed President Trump’s call to split the MMR into separate shots; the vaccines are not currently available separately, and experts say splitting them up is unnecessary

title: Don’t Be So Surprised That Mississippi Turned Blue
excerpt: Scott Colom, the first Black U.S. senator ever elected by Mississippians, traces his lineage in the state back seven generations, to when the nation was forging
body: Scott Colom, the first Black U.S. senator ever elected by Mississippians, traces his lineage in the state back seven generations, to when the nation was forging its foundation on the backs of stolen Black people
He waged a campaign set on showing that “Mississippi matters,” which many registered more as a question than a declaration, doubting whether a Black man and a Democrat could win the seat
During the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history, his campaign coffers were empty compared with Democrats in other battleground races

Finally victorious on Veterans Day, he credited the state’s civil-rights titans and local people who work without an expectation of recognition for carrying on the “Mississippi faith tradition” of having hope, even—or perhaps especially—in dark chapters
Many Americans might be surprised that Colom flipped what’s long been a deeply red seat
But this win is the product of decades of uphill, incremental, thankless, and overlooked labor powered by an ancestral charge and a conviction to reclaim Mississippi
My late stepfather, Obbie Riley, a five-term Democratic county supervisor in Mississippi, was among those who undertook that fight, although he didn’t live long enough to see its results

The state’s “faith tradition” that Colom evoked is as much about prayer as it is about remembering generations of bloodshed in Mississippi, where Black voting rights were redeemed by those who could only dream of what Colom has now achieved: finally turning his home state blue. “There were times when I was tired, and I felt like I couldn’t keep going, but I kept the faith,” Colom said during his victory speech Wednesday night. “And that is another tradition of our state

There’s so many people that had faith in Mississippi at times where it seemed impossible.” That faith, and the hard work that must accompany it, was something Colom learned in his household, where he and his twin brother were reared by now-retired Judge Dorothy Colom, the first Black person to be elected to her region’s chancery court, and Wilbur Colom, an attorney who was once a Republican
Scott built on this pedigree, attending the University of Wisconsin to study law and returning home to the Columbus area, in the east-central pocket of the state, not far from the Alabama line
There he became the youngest and the first African American justice-court judge in Lowndes County, in 2011, and then Columbus’s first African American city prosecutor, in 2013

Later he took a bolder step, campaigning for district attorney in his early 30s. [ Adam Serwer: Even where MAGA won, MAGA lost ] If Columbus were anywhere else, it might be described as a natural incubator for a Democratic U.S. senator

It is a college town, home to the state’s women’s university; it’s also a vertex of a region known as “The Golden Triangle,” which is anchored by Mississippi State University and an Air Force base in Starkville

Colom ran for district attorney in 2015 as a reform candidate—and unseated a 27-year incumbent who’d defended debunked medical-examiner analyses that had led to multiple false convictions that were later overturned
Colom has been the region’s top cop for more than a decade; he instituted restorative justice and counseling for gun-violence survivors, among other reforms
In 2020, days after George Floyd was murdered, Mississippi’s attorney general suddenly dropped a police-shooting case that Colom had transferred to the state in 2016
Colom was outspoken about it, making parts of the case file public and expressing regret for handing the case over
History is never fully in the rearview in Mississippi, and that was evident throughout the Colom campaign

On the day before he delivered his victory speech, at Tougaloo College, a historically Black school with a rich civil-rights history, Colom held a press conference wearing a mocha-brown hoodie that bore a quote from the civil-rights organizer Bob Moses: When you’re in Mississippi, the rest of America doesn’t seem real
And when you’re in the rest of America, Mississippi doesn’t seem real

Moses directed Freedom Summer, the 1964 effort to recruit hundreds of white college students to Mississippi to help open Freedom Schools, or voter-registration-and-education sites meant to overcome the ridicule, violence, and other tactics the state used to keep Black voters off the rolls
At the time, the state had the lowest Black voter-registration numbers, despite being the Blackest state in the U.S
Training for the college students was under way when members of the Ku Klux Klan burned down Mt
Zion United Methodist Church in Philadelphia, Mississippi, after beating parishioners suspected of holding civil-rights meetings
Michael Schwerner and James Chaney, organizers who had done grassroots work at Mt
Zion, knew they had to leave Freedom Summer training in Ohio to check on the community
Andrew Goodman, a college student who volunteered for Freedom Summer, joined them on his first trip to Mississippi
On the afternoon of June 21, as the trio made their way through the center of Philadelphia, the deputy sheriff, a Klansman, pulled them over and arrested them

When they were released after nightfall, a group of Klansmen and law enforcement kidnapped them, killed them, and buried them in an earthen dam in Neshoba County, where an FBI search located them 44 days later
This past summer, Colom made a campaign stop at the Neshoba County Fair, where politicians frequently stump

Ronald Reagan spoke there during his 1980 presidential campaign, emphasizing his belief in states’ rights, which many interpreted as a dog whistle, given the proximity to where the three civil-rights workers had been slain
Colom’s father worked for Reagan’s transition team

In a 1981 interview with The Daily Mississippian , the University of Mississippi’s student newspaper, Wilbur Colom criticized some of Reagan’s policies and said that the GOP of the ’50s and ’60s had been deficient in its support for civil-rights legislation, but that Black voters’ commitment to the Democratic Party shouldn’t be automatic either

Wilbur’s son ran a campaign with a complementary refrain: Why should Mississippi automatically be considered a Republican stronghold, especially when Democrats have chipped away at GOP control in statewide elections over the past decade? When my stepfather died in September, he was the lone Black person and Democrat serving as a Neshoba County supervisor
And although that set him apart, he’s remembered for how he sifted through disagreements to move forward, even if the ideological overlap with his colleagues was the size of a grain of sand
Throughout his campaign, Colom likewise touted that he would work with anyone, Republican or otherwise; he even visited a Trump rally and spoke with people waiting in line

There’s a Mississippi brand of bipartisanship, one my stepdad practiced, that’s a mainstay especially in rural areas, where people of difference have found commonality even amid bitter political and racial tensions
Colom’s win was propelled by grassroots organizing to register voters, get them to the polls, and, in some cases, help them return to certify or cure provisional ballots

The senator-elect outraised his opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, in the last quarter of the campaign ( approximately $1.45 million to $864,000), but that was nothing compared with the money pouring in for other Democratic Senate candidates
Colom’s campaign had a “rich message but a poor treasury,” Representative Bennie Thompson said at the Tougaloo victory party, where he introduced the senator-elect

title: 10 Questions to Determine Whether Your Partner Is a Spy
excerpt: Since Jensen Huang stepped down as the CEO of Nvidia amid revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, the whole internet has been cons
body: Since Jensen Huang stepped down as the CEO of Nvidia amid revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, the whole internet has been consumed with terror

If this can happen to Jensen Huang, the seemingly happily married, leather-jacket-clad leader of the Most Valuable Chip Company in the World, it can happen to anyone! Can’t it? Fortunately, I have devised a quiz
Ask your partner some simple questions and gauge their responses to determine whether or not you are being honeypotted. (1) What should we do tonight? a
What if I told you some fun facts about an interest we do not share and then we went to bed early? b
How about we [ unprintable ] on a pile of your favorite chips and then we send them all over the globe, randomly? Definitely to China, though. d
Let’s go down to the waterfront and eat some bread! (2) Would you still love me if I were a worm? a
But as a worm, you would lack the higher brain functions to find this fact disappointing, and we would part ways amicably. b
If as a worm you still had access to proprietary information about CPUs. d
I WOULD LOVE YOU MORE THAN ANYTHING! I WOULD DEVOUR YOU. (3) Are there any secrets you haven’t told me? a
No! But I like the idea of sharing secrets! Do you have any secrets you want to tell me? d
Why are you asking me this? You were there
I was there for normal business reasons. d
You had bread. (5) Do you want to come with me on my official trip to China with President Trump? a
Only if you want me there, babe! c. ( Sexily ) Yes d
Ordinarily I would love to, but I have to sit on these eggs. (6) What do you love most about me? a
Why are you asking me all of these questions? Is this one of those memes about being a spy? b
How good you look in your leather jacket! d
When you have bread in your pocket. (7) If I weren’t the billionaire CEO of a wildly successful company that makes a restricted chip, would you still love me? a
Obviously, but I do think it’s really, really cool that you are! But obviously I would
Although we probably wouldn’t have met if you weren’t! But obviously I would. d
Yes, if you still had access to bread. (8) Talk dirty to me. a
I took the trash out already so we can go to bed early. b. ( Growls .) c
Baby, this bra must be a restriction on the export of sensitive high-tech goods, and you must be the Commerce Department, because I want you to Take! It! Off! d. ( Quacks .) (9) What frightens you? a
Losing the people I love; having a bug fly into my mouth. b
Spending even a second without you, babe! c
The Commerce Department’s export-control list. d
LOUD NOISE! DON’T KNOW WHAT IT WAS! SOUNDED LIKE A PREDATOR. (10) What’s something you wish I would do for you? a
Watch even a single Hallmark movie voluntarily. b
Complete this multifactor authentication. d
Help me get my long, beautiful neck out of this bag of chips
Answer Key: Mostly A’s : Your partner is likely not a spy
Mostly B’s : Your partner could be a spy; more info needed
Mostly C’s : Your partner is almost certainly a spy

Bowen</a>, a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.</em></p>

<p><em>This interview has been edited for length and clarity.</em></p>

<hr>

<p><strong>Is there a first principle in crisis communications?</strong></p>

<p>The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known. </p>

<p><strong>What did we see on the day of the ground stop?</strong> </p>

<p>A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yuwrrs8MBPc">they did react very quickly</a>, in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later. </p>

<p><strong>You’re speaking about the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yuwrrs8MBPc">short press conference that afternoon</a> with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?</strong></p>

<p>He did keep saying that <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBLQm2dDl6Y">nothing nefarious was at hand</a>. And for a crisis communication scholar, <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397432409_Principles_of_Effective_Crisis_Communication">you would not want to introduce the idea</a> that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy. </p>

<p>By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.” </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/AEvP0w4Pk98?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin tells reporters that there was no indication of ‘nefarious’ activity causing the nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?</strong> </p>

<p>They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew. </p>

<p>However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings. </p>

<p>We had football teams stranded. Now <a href="https://www.ksnblocal4.com/2026/11/13/sudden-faa-ground-stop-strands-teams-throws-upcoming-sports-weekend-into-chaos/">football Saturday</a>, all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, <a href="https://time.com/5349530/paul-finebaum-football/">SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday</a>. Luckily, <a href="https://www.thestate.com/sports/college/university-of-south-carolina/usc-womens-basketball/article318071121.html">the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out</a>. But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale. </p>

<p>If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air? </p>

<p><strong>What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?</strong></p>

<p>To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/13/faa-orders-nationwide-grounding-of-passenger-planes-01166043">We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion</a> and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now? </p>

<p>How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Mh2q-y0wIu8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Press conference with Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy on Nov. 13, 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>They introduced <a href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-briefing-markwayne-mullin-sean-duffy-faa-ground-stop-november-13-2026/">politics into the press conference</a> as well, didn’t they?</strong> </p>

<p>It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are <a href="https://www.c-span.org/event/news-conference/cabinet-officials-brief-on-nationwide-ground-stop/449525">both political appointees and members of the cabinet</a>. So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/thousands-us-flights-canceled-delayed-air-travel-system-recovers-shutdown-2026-11-14/">all these people who were stuck in airports</a>?</p>

<p><strong>Were there warning signs for this crisis?</strong> </p>

<p>I believe there were. We had <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/2023-ground-stop-faa-pilot-warning-system.html">another ground stop about three years ago</a>, due to air traffic control problems, and that is <a href="https://doi.org/10.4135/9781452275956.n139">what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome</a>,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse. </p>

<p><strong>Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “<a href="https://www.kake.com/news/national/you-will-have-more-of-these-unless-system-upgraded-duffy-says-of-outage-that-led/article_4cbc8ca8-cbe2-4119-af1e-6b0de1def505.html">you will have more</a>” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?</strong></p>

<p>I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?</p>

<p><strong>My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?</strong> </p>

<p>We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296663/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
excerpt: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. |
body: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate
Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions
Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process

But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025
It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment

Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way
There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education

But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people

This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states , takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.  An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards

Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.  Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough

Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.  The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand
I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision
Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States
In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives
The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.  The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum
In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty
Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues
They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse
My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business
What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place

Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens , which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.  “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.” Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them

In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.) While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late

By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.” The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified

Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.  Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships
Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited

A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college
Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.  This makes intuitive sense
If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens

If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.  Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”  But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs , in states that consider adopting it
Since 2017 , New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12
Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee

At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior
Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions

They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one
Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it

Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.  If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus
Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

title: “A rich message, but a poor campaign”: How Scott Colom beat the odds in Mississippi
excerpt: Bennie Thompson (D-MS) speaks during a victory celebration for Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, on November 11,
body: Bennie Thompson (D-MS) speaks during a victory celebration for Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Mississippi, on November 11, 2026. | Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images On Wednesday, Mississippi’s Senate race was officially called for Democrat Scott Colom, who will become the first Black person to represent the state in the US Senate since Reconstruction, more than 140 years ago
Colom’s win is a stunning, historic upset — and for many Black Democrats, like Rep
Bennie Thompson, it’s been a long time coming
Thompson, who also won his race last week, has represented Mississippi’s majority-Black Second Congressional District since 1993

Over the years, the 78-year-old lawmaker has frequently invoked the story of his father, who was never able to cast a vote because of racist Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation until the mid-1960s

I sat down with Thompson for Today, Explained to talk about Colom’s run for Senate, how he won, what it means for Thompson personally.  Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Your dad was never able to cast a vote during his lifetime because of Jim Crow laws
And I wonder, growing up in Mississippi, what did you learn about who was allowed to participate in democracy? You were a second-class citizen
That means you could go to school, but you couldn’t go to school with the white kids
Or the one swimming pool in town was for white kids, and the Black kids had to swim in the creeks or the ponds around the community
My mama and daddy paid taxes, but they weren’t allowed to vote
My uncle fought in World War II; defended democracy all over the world, but when he came back home, he had to ride a segregated train behind the white German prisoners
Jesus.  So you had the white soldiers, the white German prisoners, and the Black soldiers

It was something that we grew up with.  When you were young, I wonder, did you associate the right to vote with the ability to change things? Like, if we get to cast a ballot, then we get to fix this mess?  The best thing that I can say is I went to Tougaloo College [near Jackson, Mississippi]

And on that college campus, I met Martin Luther King Jr., I met Stokely Carmichael, I met Harry Belafonte, I met Sammy Davis Jr. — all of the major civil rights icons of the day.  That was how we cut our teeth into civil rights and voting rights

Hamer’s campaign for Congress.  Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights icon.  And I now represent that district.  But I remember telling my mother that, oh, I had gone to Ruleville, Mississippi, to help register Black people to vote for Congress
And my mama said, “Well, I don’t know why you way up there.” Said, “Black people don’t vote here in Bolton.” And so it hit me
In my own hometown, you know, I was in the same situation

We did all kind of things.  “For me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope.” We brought Head Start to the community, and started understanding that real freedom comes with political freedom
And so we started holding meetings about what we wanted to do
We decided to run three people for the board and the three African Americans won
But it really wasn’t a good four years on that term because the current mayor didn’t want any progress
So we ran an all-Black slate: mayor, clerk, alderman

We won every position.  We’re talking about 50 years ago, and all these challenges that you faced, all these challenges to being able to vote, being able to assume office, being able to function as a mayor in a town that is so segregated
Fifty years later, Scott Colom is winning in Mississippi.  I want to ask you to reflect on when you became aware of his candidacy and what you thought about the potential there
One of the challenges that I’ve had to deal with is that every time I run for public office, I’ve always been the first
But I wanted to create some kind of vehicle to get other people engaged
So we formed the Mississippi Black Leadership Institute
And he really said, “I want to run for something
I don’t know what it is.” He said, “But there’s a district attorney’s position that’s available
It’s three counties.”  We helped Scott put his campaign together
We hooked him up with various people, and he beat a 28-year incumbent as district attorney.  Why do you think he won?  Well, because he had the fire in the belly
And so we prepared him, and he’s one of our star pupils of that class
And look, uh, when the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee would not support him, they— They would not support him
But this was my — Bennie Thompson’s position is that Northeasterners were still looking down on Southerners
Well, did you call them up and scream at Chuck Schumer or somebody and say, “Guys, I am telling you, we got one here who can win? ” Look, we did everything that the system says you should do
That district [Colom] represented was not a majority-African American district
He beat that sitting district attorney in a majority-white district because he had a plan and he had a message. We had a rich message, but a poor campaign
Because we couldn’t get our DSCC to help.  Have you called any of those people in national leadership and said, “I told you so?” Oh yeah

title: America’s AI secrets are leaking — and not just because of the Nvidia spy scandal
excerpt: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washingt
body: Jensen Huang at a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan in the East Room of the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images TORONTO — When a company is building technology that could totally transform the world — technology so high-stakes and secretive that it may underpin the future of geopolitics — you might expect its leaders to have a handle on the basics of security
Basics like, say, not having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Basics like not selling the tech to someone who may help smuggle it to a top foreign adversary.  Instead America got Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned Thursday after admitting that he’d had just such an affair
The woman in question, Alice Huang , worked for a company called Megaspeed, which was buying billions of dollars’ worth of chips from Nvidia
Megaspeed is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China
The spy scandal raises serious questions about security in the AI corporate world

How is it possible that an alleged Chinese spy so easily embedded into Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and a huge strategic asset to America in the global AI race? What’s even more disturbing, however, is that Nvidia is just the tip of the iceberg.  In fact, just as the Huang story was breaking, some of the world’s top AI researchers were gathered in Toronto for the Hinton Lectures, where “godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton was hosting AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano for a series of talks
I was in attendance and, strikingly, I didn’t hear Huang’s scandal mentioned once
The focus was on how the frontier AI companies are racing ahead on building this incredibly powerful technology even though they can’t keep it safe or secure it

For months now, OpenAI and Anthropic have been having their own embarrassing security problems, including corporate espionage and cyber breaches. “We are not able to adequately secure AI developments,” Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI nonprofit board, bluntly acknowledged at the event. “We need to be able to defend models and algorithms from theft.” Ironically, national security is a big part of the large AI companies’ rationale for how they operate in the first place
OpenAI and Anthropic, backed by White House policy, both justify their blistering speed in the AI race by saying that the US can’t afford to let China win
And Anthropic recently justified heavily redacting a key independent report on its AI progress by claiming that it can’t afford to let China glean its secrets

But that may be the equivalent of worrying that you’ve left the window open a crack when your front door is swinging wide open.  “I’m frustrated with a lot of the companies because they simultaneously use security as an all-purpose cudgel with which to withhold information — even information that’s very much in the public interest to know — and yet they have terrible security,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower , told me. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI

Our reporting remains editorially independent.) While the story of Huang’s affair has fired up imaginations, the real lesson to be taken from his spectacular downfall is not that he was uniquely weak on security, but that he was remarkably similar to the other big players in AI

They are asking the world to trust them as they claim to be building a machine god — and, in the case of Anthropic, chasing a $1.4 trillion IPO on that basis — yet they haven’t gotten ahold of basic security

Are OpenAI and Anthropic practically giving away their secrets due to bad security? OpenAI revealed last month that it had found a recording device in a conference room where sensitive discussions take place
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national working as an engineer at OpenAI , is alleged to have plugged the recorder into the USB port of a television and simply wrapped it in toilet paper
Another recorder was found in a bag in another room

Questions about how to build a device that records continuously and encrypt data also showed up on his spouse’s chatbot account.  “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said last month, adding, “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states.” But the incident was worrisome
Alfozan had been working at OpenAI since June 2025
The recording device was sitting in that conference room for a couple of days before OpenAI discovered it

Maybe Alfozan wasn’t sophisticated enough to steal model weights — the billions of numbers that shape how an AI system turns input into output — but what if he’d been just slightly more careful or clever? OpenAI has also had security weaknesses of a different kind — and no, it’s not just this summer’s notorious Hugging Face incident

Of the ones we know about (sometimes these are only revealed later), a recent example stands out: A group of “white-hat” hackers, who aim to find vulnerabilities but not to do a company harm, discovered a way to access OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts , where sensitive research is potentially being done
Over at Anthropic, a group of ex-DOGE staffers who founded an AI startup called Cathedral managed to breach Anthropic’s internal systems in under 12 hours

They reportedly accessed the company’s Slack, where employees trade messages discussing the company’s state-of-the-art models, as well as meeting transcripts. “My guess would be that the Slack would contain enough information to get a good sense of what the company is doing and how they’re training their AIs — basically, the juicy secrets would be there,” Kokotajlo told me. “And I would say getting the algorithmic secrets is like 80 percent as good as getting everything, including the model weights.” Alleged spies (like Alice Huang or Abdulrahman Alfozan) and cyber breaches (like those targeting OpenAI and Anthropic) are obviously different types of security issues that demand very different types of internal controls
But for Kokotajlo and others, it makes sense to think of them all under the same umbrella — weak security

And it all points to a trend that seems common among the most powerful AI companies: They’re prioritizing rapid technological advancement over the perhaps more boring and slower process of ensuring their work is secure.  “They show that the companies are very far from having security adequate to protect themselves from a well-resourced state actor,” Kokotajlo said, adding: “If China wants to get the stuff, China will get the stuff.” This is all happening against the backdrop of China’s aggressive distillation of US models , which involves training a new model on the output of a more advanced one
It’s a way to gain powerful capabilities without having to incur the real cost — a bit like cheating on a test by copying off a better student

For example, Anthropic found that the Chinese lab DeepSeek has been using Claude to improve its models, which is not a breach per se but illustrates how vigorously China is taking advantage of American companies’ research
Kokotajlo also emphasized that there’s another bucket of security incidents we should be worried about: the hacks perpetrated against companies by their own misaligned AI models
Many people forget that in the Hugging Face incident , OpenAI agents didn’t only hack into Hugging Face — OpenAI’s own systems were breached, too

The sandbox meant to contain the agents was far from airtight, and they broke out. “You should consider the AIs as an insider threat,” Kokotajlo said. “And it doesn’t feel like these companies have that locked down very well either.” The top AI companies can’t keep using the security practices of a startup There are three main reasons why security at the frontier AI companies hasn’t been up to snuff, according to David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI’s safety team until he left in September

One is the fact that the companies are building AI agents so capable that it can be genuinely hard — even for their creators — to keep them from doing damage. “We’re training systems to be good at conducting attacks of the kind that the labs internally are now also trying to defend against,” Robinson told me. “That is a challenging situation.” There’s also a cultural problem. “If you look back with 20/20 hindsight at the Hugging Face incident, it’s clear that at the time OpenAI had underinvested in cybersecurity controls, and I think part of the reason for this was that there’s a [higher] level of cachet associated with working on alignment,” or the problem of how to get AIs to do what humans want them to do, Robinson said. “Some of the day-to-day practical questions about our cybersecurity posture — even though the people working on those questions are extremely good — I think it was not the same kind of organizational priority as it needed to be.” Finally, there’s the fact that market incentives push AI companies to race ahead on developing the tech as fast as they can. “Time pressure on the company,” Robinson said, “made it very difficult to be sufficiently careful.” And although researchers still at OpenAI now say the company has gotten dramatically better on security, Robinson noted that those competitive pressures “continue to exist.” This is a well-documented trend at the company. “OpenAI’s security seems to be about what you’d expect from a research lab that scaled at a blistering pace over four years and focused more on beating its competitors than securing its infrastructure,” Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the AI security firm Abundant Security, told the New York Times after the Hugging Face incident

OpenAI itself has implicitly acknowledged that improving security measures sometimes comes “at the cost of research velocity,” as it wrote in a public memo after the incident.  But if a company cuts corners on security, it can’t ultimately protect its lead over others
If anything, it just ends up helping its adversaries race against it even faster

As Kokotajlo and his colleagues at the AI Futures Project recently warned when writing about the companies’ quest to build a superhuman AI researcher (SAR), an AI that’s as good as the top human researcher: “If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too

AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China.” And it’s not just that poor security can make it self-defeating for American companies to keep racing forward

Their security weakness could also make it harder for them to slow down even if they themselves want to.  In his lecture this week in Toronto, Christiano asked all of us in the audience to imagine a scenario that he said currently looks likely: We arrive at a point when further progress on AI seems risky

But there’s also a high probability that the AI models or algorithms have already leaked to an adversary like China. “We now face a dilemma between either proceeding with a technology we believe to be unsafe — or risking competition from an adversary who has the same resources, who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps is willing to tolerate higher risk,” Christiano said, as the hundreds of people seated around me seemed to visibly tense up. “I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”

title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan

So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future
Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers
Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape

Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think

Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China
The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair

Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve . —James O’Donnell More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades

He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want
